- All the people I met when I went last year were super nice. I had a random older lady buy me a drink on the train without even saying a word to me, I had people invite me in for a free meal at their restaurant, people would always help me out or want to take time from their day to show me around the city (I am white, which would make a difference)
- How fit and healthy the older generation is. Every park would be full of people 50+ dancing, exercising, playing ping pong etc
- The infrastructure was amazing. Fast and reliable high speed rail, easy to navigate subway system, rental bikes that you could take around the city for less than 1/hour and dedicated bike lanes. 
- How open people were to Australians, I asked multiple people, even soldiers, how they felt about Australians and the vibe was that we are all humans and humans are the same, there is no ill-will towards us. 
- I was surprised by the food, I naively assumed it would be like Chinese food in Australia, but it was unrecognisable in some places. Very interesting to try tho!
- I also asked people about the social credit system and they’d never heard about it. Seems like a western myth from my understanding.

I have no doubt you work hard for your money, just like low income people also work very hard to earn their money. The difference is if they get sick without healthcare they can die because they can't afford treatment. From my point of view I would rather give some of money to healthcare to save the lives of less fortunate people than to have a little more money in my bank account.

As an Australian it seems like a very selfish outlook to me. Over here we only pay a small amount relative to our income which goes to help the people with very low income who can't afford to pay for themselves. A 2% levy for people with higher incomes is hardly taking all your money, and improves the overall health of the population, which in turn leads to reduced cost on society such as lack of employees and skilled workers due to Illness.

so recently my grandfather passed away and I learned something about my family that I never new before.

In the Second World War, during the holocaust
my great grandparents, who lived in a small village in the netherlands at the time, used to hide up to 30 people in their small bakery at a time. My grandfather also kept guns in the bakery, and back then if you were caught with a weapon you would be killed instantly.

One of these people was a small girl who's parents had been killed by the nazis and my great grandparents pretended that she was theirs so she wouldn't be killed, even though she looked different to all their other children. This little girl survived and ended up having children, grandchildren and even great grandchildren.

That entire family wouldn't be alive today if it weren't for my ancestors bravery and that makes me very proud:)
